Where We Are

Part III connects stored data to predictions, answers, and actions

Outline: ML Systems

01 · Preparing Examples

Why ML SystemsA useful model also needs reliable data, predictions and feedback

The model is one component of a system that must keep working

From Data to a Checked ModelPrepare model inputs, learn from past outcomes, then check predictions

The pipeline connects data preparation to training and evaluation

Separate ML PipelinesFeature preparation, training and prediction can run on different schedules

A shared feature definition connects pipelines that run at different times

§ Prediction Rows

Failure Prediction ExampleAt 10:00, predict whether P-17 will fail during the next hour

The 10:48 failure becomes the label for the 10:00 prediction

Features and LabelsFeatures are model inputs and the label is the observed outcome

The model predicts a label that has not arrived yet

The Next-Hour LabelA label answers a question about one future time interval

The 10:48 failure belongs to the earlier prediction window

Training ExamplesOne row combines past inputs with the outcome that followed

Each row describes one P-17 prediction, rather than the whole machine

§ Available Inputs

Feature AvailabilityEvent: when it happened. Available: when the system could read it

FeatureEventAvailableValue
temperature09:5509:5631
alarm_count09:5810:123
vibration09:5009:510.8
The alarm happened before 10:00 but arrived at 10:12

Late Feature ArrivalAn earlier event can still be unknown when the model predicts

Only temperature and vibration are available before the prediction line

Caveat: Future InformationUsing a late input during training gives the model information it would lack

The late alarm would make the training example unrealistically informative

Demo: Available InputsRun the join, then exclude inputs that arrived after 10:00

  1. Join Predictions and Features using machine_id; filter event_at ≤ predicted_at.
  2. Also filter available_at ≤ predicted_at. Which feature disappears?
Ctrl/⌘ + Enter
Query result
Write a query on the left, then Run

Answer: Available InputsBoth time conditions must hold for the input to be usable

SELECT p.id, f.feature, f.value
FROM Predictions p JOIN Features f ON f.machine_id=p.machine_id
WHERE f.event_at <= p.predicted_at AND f.available_at <= p.predicted_at
ORDER BY p.id, f.feature;
idfeaturevalue
prediction_42temperature31.0
prediction_42vibration0.8
The late alarm report is excluded

Available Model InputsThe filtered result reconstructs what the predictor could actually read

The two remaining values are the inputs for the 10:00 prediction

02 · Making Predictions

§ Learning from History

Training and PredictionTraining learns from known outcomes and prediction uses the saved model

The model learns from past labels and predicts a future label

Batch InferenceCompute a set of predictions ahead of the time they will be read

The pipeline writes a prediction table that applications can read later

Request-Time InferenceCalculate a prediction when a request arrives

Request-time serving needs both available features and the saved model

Training, Validation and TestFit on training data, select with validation, and reserve the test for the final check

The three sets have different jobs; the percentages are one illustrative split

Overlapping Label WindowsSplitting prediction rows can still let the same future failure cross the boundary

The same 10:48 failure labels rows on both sides of the split

Checking Later ExamplesCheck the model on later examples that it did not learn from

Past training data and later checking data serve different purposes

Predictions and OutcomesA prediction is correct only when it matches the observed label

Three of the four predictions match their observed outcomes

Accuracy and Missed FailuresA high overall accuracy can hide the failures the system was built to detect

Always normal: 5 misses; detector: 2 misses + 8 false alarms
The 95% model misses every failure in this illustrative set of 100 cases

Error Costs and a DecisionCompare errors using the operational cost of each outcome

Prediction policyMissed failuresFalse alarmsIllustrative total cost
Always normal505 × 100 = 500
Failure detector282 × 100 + 8 × 1 = 208
The preferred model changes when the costs of errors are included

§ Shared Feature Meaning

A Temperature FeatureA feature definition tells us how source readings become one input

Both paths turn the same readings into the value 31

Caveat: Different CalculationsA last reading and a mean can share a name while carrying different meanings

Training receives 31 while prediction receives 32 from the same readings

Shared Feature MeaningKeep the calculation and the unit the same in both paths

The model receives the same kind of input during training and prediction

Reproducible ML AssetsRecover the data, feature definition and model version behind a prediction

A model file alone does not recover the inputs that produced it

The Same Weights, Different InputsChanging the feature rule can change the prediction without changing the model

31 ≤ 31.5 → normal; 32 > 31.5 → alarm
The mean produces normal; the last reading produces an alarm with unchanged weights

03 · Checking Results

§ Prediction Records

Prediction RecordKeep the input and prediction so the later outcome can be matched

The 10:00 prediction is recorded before its outcome is known

Observed OutcomeAttach the observed failure to the prediction it answers

The 10:48 failure confirms the recorded prediction p-42

Feature and Prediction LogsKeep evidence that can reconnect a prediction with its input and later label

Prediction logs let later outcomes be matched to the earlier decision

Delayed OutcomesRecent predictions may still have missing outcomes

The same ten predictions score differently as more labels arrive

§ Model Updates

Input Changes and QualityCheck what changed before deciding to train a new model

A unit change needs an input fix before any model update

Candidate ComparisonCompare the current model and a candidate on the same later examples

The candidate matches eight outcomes while the current model matches six

MLOps: A Repeating CycleDevelop a model, use it, observe outcomes and improve the next candidate

Operating the model continues after the first deployment

Model UpdateUse observed examples to train and check a candidate before replacing the model

A checked candidate can replace v1 while v1 remains available

A Limited Model ReleaseKeep the baseline and compare observed outcomes before widening a release

Model and feature versions move together through the release decision

Takeaway: Operate with available data

1Reconstruct available inputs and keep train, validation and test roles separate
2Preserve feature definitions and compare the costs of prediction errors
3Link versions, predictions and mature labels before releasing an update
